items.name: part_1
items.direction: Narrate this for a premium documentary YouTube channel about money, history and the tricks behind them. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller with a hint of mystery: curious, quietly amused, never slow, never announcer-like. Natural emphasis on dates and numbers, a short pause before each question, a beat of comic timing before and after each light joke. Energetic and punchy on the opening lines. Keep the same voice, pace and energy from start to finish. Chars voices two funny cartoon characters (a smug gold bar and a nervous banknote), short and punchy, performed exactly as described in each bracket.
lines: You have been robbed of gold! You heard that right! This happened when your money stopped being backed by gold! So what is it backed by?
Look at the small print on a British pound, or an Indian rupee: "I promise to pay the bearer." Pay you what?
In early 1933, a hundred-dollar bill was a claim on almost five ounces of gold. By the 1960s, less than three. Today, spend it on gold, and you'd get about a fortieth of an ounce.
Somewhere between those numbers is one Sunday night in 1971, when that promise quietly changed... and never changed back.
[smug, deep, rich] Spoiler: it's not me anymore.
So let's follow one banknote through twenty-six centuries of money, and find out what's really standing behind yours.

Before there was a note, there was a problem. You have chickens. You want a goat. The owner hates chickens. Economists call this the double coincidence of wants. Everyone else calls it a wasted afternoon.
So people tried shells, cattle, metal... and one material kept winning. Gold.
It doesn't rust. It doesn't rot. It's rare, but not too rare. You can melt it, split it and stamp it. And everyone, everywhere, already wanted it.

More than twenty-five centuries ago, in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, were stamped with a lion's head. They're among the earliest coins we know of. No more weighing metal at every sale. You could just count.
But gold had one big problem. It's heavy. Try buying a house with a backpack full of coins. So paper slipped in through the back door.
[smug] Told you paper couldn't be trusted.

lines: About a thousand years ago, in Sichuan, China, the local coins were made of iron. Heavy, and not worth much. Carrying your savings meant carrying a small anvil.

So merchants left their coins with trusted shops and carried paper receipts instead, called jiaozi. When some of those shops went bust, the Song government took over. In 1024, it issued what's often called the world's first government paper money.
Then it discovered the oldest temptation in money. If paper works... why not print a little more? More notes. Higher prices.
[sheepish] In my defence, they printed me.
That's the first mirage in this story: paper only works while people believe what's printed on it.

Europe caught on later. From 1694, Bank of England notes promised to pay the bearer, and for much of the next two centuries, you really could swap them for gold. Paper was the ticket. Gold sat in the vault. That's a gold standard.
Sounds perfect. So why did every country eventually walk away from it?
Here's the catch. Money could only grow as fast as the gold pile. And in a panic, everyone wants their gold back at the same moment. There's never enough for everyone at once.
So in wars and crises, countries kept suspending the promise. Britain broke the link for good in 1931.

America went further. On April 5th, 1933, in the depths of the Great Depression, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 6102. Americans had to hand in most of their gold coins, bars and gold certificates by May 1st, paid at the official price of 20 dollars 67 cents an ounce.
Hoard it, and you risked a 10,000-dollar fine, ten years in prison, or both. Imagine explaining that one at a dinner party.

A year later, the official price jumped to 35 dollars. Same gold. But each dollar now stood for about 41 percent less of it. Our hundred-dollar bill? Its claim fell from almost five ounces to under three.

And Americans couldn't legally own gold bars again until the last day of 1974. But here's the loophole. Ordinary people were locked out of gold. Foreign governments weren't. And that loophole is what eventually broke the whole system.

lines: July 1944. The Second World War is still raging, and delegates from 44 countries check into a hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. Not for a holiday.

The plan: other currencies peg to the dollar, and the dollar pegs to gold at 35 dollars an ounce, swappable by foreign governments. Why the dollar? Because in the early post-war years, America held roughly three quarters of the world's official gold.
Suddenly the dollar was as good as gold, and better in one way. You could earn interest on dollars. Gold just sits there, looking expensive.

But there was a trap built in. To give the world enough dollars, America had to keep sending them abroad. The more dollars piled up overseas, the less American gold could cover them. The economist Robert Triffin warned about this in 1959. It's now called the Triffin dilemma.

France noticed. In January 1965, it announced it would swap at least 300 million of its dollars for American gold. Its finance minister, Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, had a name for America's position: an "exorbitant privilege."
America plugged the leaks with a shared gold pool in London and emergency deals between central banks. In March 1968, the gold pool collapsed. The dam was cracking.

Before we get to that Sunday night: every money trick in this story worked because people didn't look closely. Looking closely is the whole point of Money Mirage. If that's your thing, subscribe. Now... Camp David.
August 1971. President Richard Nixon takes his economic team to Camp David for the weekend. And on Sunday night, August 15th, he goes on television.
A 90-day freeze on wages and prices. A 10 percent surcharge on imports. And the big one: the gold window was closed. Foreign governments could no longer swap their dollars for American gold.
It never came back. By 1973, the major currencies were floating, priced by markets instead of metal. Our hundred-dollar bill was now backed by no gold at all.
Which leaves a puzzle. The dollar lost its last link to gold more than fifty years ago. You'd expect the world to dump it. Instead, it became even more powerful. Why?

lines: Part of it is oil. In 1974, the US and Saudi Arabia reached an informal understanding: Saudi oil money flowed into US government bonds, and America offered military support. No treaty ever forced oil into dollars, but oil has mostly been priced in dollars ever since.

The bigger reason is a network effect. It's why your whole family ends up on the same messaging app, including the uncle who only sends good-morning memes. If every bank, exporter and central bank already uses dollars, the easiest thing for you to do is use dollars too.

The numbers are wild. In April 2025, the dollar was on one side of about 89 percent of all currency trades, in a market moving roughly 9.6 trillion dollars a day. Central banks keep about 57 percent of their foreign reserves in dollars. The euro, in second place, sits around 21.
But gold never really left. Central banks bought more than a thousand tonnes of it in each of 2022, 2023 and 2024, and another 863 tonnes in 2025.
So why not just go back to gold? Here's the problem. All the gold ever mined, about 222,600 tonnes, would fit in a single cube roughly 22.6 metres on each side.

Tie the world's money to that cube, and money can only grow as fast as miners can dig. In a crisis, central banks' hands are tied. Many economists, including former Fed chair Ben Bernanke, argue that's part of what made the Great Depression so brutal: the longer a country clung to gold, the deeper it sank.

So, back to the question we started with. What is your money backed by? Read that promise on the note again. Today, the Bank of England says its notes can only be exchanged for... other Bank of England notes.

What really stands behind it is trust. Trust that the central bank keeps prices stable. Trust in a government that collects taxes in that currency. And trust that everyone else will still accept it tomorrow.
Gold was a promise you could hold. Paper is a promise you have to believe. And the moment enough people stop believing... that's when the mirage disappears.

That's the trick behind every note in your wallet. And money has plenty more: prices, deals and scams that aren't what they seem. Seeing through them is what this channel is for. Subscribe to Money Mirage, and next time, we'll see through another one.
